name: toast
description:
Something happened, said briefly and out of the way. 15 uses across the app and avenID. The rule it carries: feedback may not outrun the truth — a toast saying `Draft created` while the list still shows the same items is a lie the user catches immediately.

The `placement: inline` variant is what the legacy `alert` class becomes. That class is used by checkout and avenID for an error beside the thing that failed, not a transient notification — and until this existed, neither surface could migrate off it without losing the distinction.

base.$description:
CONTAINER. This unit establishes an inline-size container named after itself, so anything inside it can respond to the width of THIS BOX rather than to the width of the window. That is the difference that matters for a design system: a composite dropped into a 320px sidebar and the same composite on a 320px phone are the same situation, and a viewport query calls them different ones. The library carries no viewport media query anywhere for exactly this reason — the only `@media` in it is `prefers-reduced-motion`, which is a person's setting and not a size.

`inline-size: 100%` is the container's REQUIRED companion, not a preference. `container-type: inline-size` makes the box's width independent of its contents — that is the containment being asked for — so a container with no width of its own has nothing left to size from and collapses to zero. This unit did: centred in a grid it became a column of single words. A container fills what it is given and bounds itself with `max-inline-size`; it never sizes to its text.

`calc(100% - 2rem)` rather than `100vw`, for the same reason as the modal: `vw` counts the scrollbar, and a toast two pixels too wide gives the page a horizontal scrollbar it did not have before.

IT DECLARES `--icon-tint`, the colour the engine paints a duotone's secondary layer with. Declared HERE, on the unit that draws the glyph, and not once at the document root: a global custom property is the anti-pattern the whole scoping design exists to avoid — two brands on one page write the same name and the second wins. An app shell is no better, because a shell is a container that may host more than one vibe. A unit is the smallest thing that owns its own subtree, so the tint travels with the component that needs it and reaches nothing else.

body.$description: `overflow-wrap:anywhere` because a toast routinely carries an id, a URL or an email — one unbreakable token sets the element's min-content width and pushes the toast past the viewport.

error.$description: An error inline is `role=alert`, which interrupts — correct for something the user must act on. The same tone floating as a toast is `role=status`, which does not. The placement decides the role.

placement.$description: Where it lives, and it changes what the thing IS. A toast floats and leaves; an inline alert stays beside what it belongs to. Both surfaces that still use the legacy `alert` class use it for the second kind — an error the user must act on — and a toast that vanishes takes its instruction with it. This is the variant that unblocks their migration.

inline.$description: In the flow, full width, no shadow, no dismiss. It belongs to the thing above it and stays until that thing changes.

reducedMotion.$description: The entrance may fade but must never be the only thing that reveals the text — a toast whose content arrives via a transform is a toast that is invisible under `reduce` if the transform is dropped.

a11y.note: `role=status` with `aria-live=polite` announces without interrupting. An ERROR that the user must act on is not a toast — it belongs beside the thing that failed, because a toast that vanishes takes the instruction with it. The dismiss button is a real button with a label; 1.5rem is under the 24px target minimum on its own, so it relies on the toast's padding as hit area and must keep it.
